newsitem.title: GERMANY: Finland's Lipponen wants strict EMU reading.
newsitem.headline: Finland's Lipponen wants strict EMU reading.

text.p: Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said in an interview released on Tuesday that Helsinki would insist on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty governing European monetary union (EMU).
"We are putting pressure, along with other countries, on those states that do not fulfil the convergence criteria," Lipponen told Die Zeit.
"We have met the standards, so anyone who wants to join in must do so too -- and without any tricks," Lipponen added in an interview from the newspaper's Wednesday edition.

Addressing fears in some countries that the admission of Italy to the EMU starting line-up in 1999 might undermine the strength of the euro, Lipponen said: "It would only be good for countries like Italy if we take a hard line.
"Prime Minister Romano Prodi has all my sympathy. His government really offers hope for Italy and Europe -- if he doesn't make it then no-one else will," Lipponen said.
"And if the Italians make demonstrable efforts, then the decision over the currency union cannot be a question of tenths of a percentage point."

Independent economists expect Italy to miss the Maastricht treaty budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product this year, despite strenuous efforts including the levying of a one-off "euro-tax".
Lipponen also warned Germany would suffer if the single currency is not realised.
"There would be an enormous revaluation of the German mark, and that would harm the German economy most of all and destroy many German jobs," Lipponen said.
